title: Validity and accuracy of impulse-response models for modeling and predicting training effects on performance of swimmers
population: 11 swimmers followed for 61 weeks across two competitive seasons; daily load from pool kilometres and dry-land equivalents weighted by intensity; performance from 50-m trials twice weekly
findings: Six impulse-response models, including Banister (Ba), variable dose-response (Bu) and indirect-response models, were ranked by Akaike information criterion; Ba and Bu had the greatest Akaike weights (0.339 +/- 0.254 and 0.360 +/- 0.296).

Trained on the first 20 weeks, mean absolute percentage error was 2.02 +/- 0.65% (Ba) and 2.17 +/- 0.65% (Bu) on the next 8 weeks, and 2.69 +/- 1.23% (Ba) and 2.56 +/- 0.79% (Bu) on the following season.

The authors concluded that, although the top two models approximated the training-performance relationship, their ability to predict future performance from past data was not satisfactory for individual training planning.
limitations: Swimming, 11 athletes, short sprint performance. The comparison of the 2-3% error with the size of meaningful performance changes is the verifier's interpretation, not stated in the abstract.
implications: Treat model forecasts as uncertain: expose prediction error bands (order of 2-3% MAPE in this dataset) and never present a point forecast of race time as reliable from this model alone.
Select among Banister variants by information criterion plus a held-out forward test; do not rely on in-sample R2. Banister and variable dose-response performed about equally.

verification.notes: Crossref confirms title, MSSE, 2023-02-07. All numbers match Europe PMC abstract. Removed an unsupported claim from limitations (relation of 2-3% to meaningful performance change) and flagged it as interpretation.
